1.Text: During the time of this event, I was the On-the-job Training Instructor (OJTI) for our Radar East position training Person A. We were on for about an hour already at the time. While traffic volume was not high, there had been increased complexity with Parachute Jump Area (PJA) happening, and multiple VFR and primary targets that were a factor with our traffic that we were not in contact with. There was a visual identification tagged aircraft flying over ZZZ airport at 056 and Local Control (LC) (training in progress at the time) called asking if we wanted their next departure capped at 040 for them, which we said yes to. That cap was to stop a TCAS-RA from happening. We were discussing at the time if the cap was necessary or not. Aircraft X was put on course direct to ZZZ [VOR]. We got distracted with other things, and Aircraft X leveled at 040 towards the 044 MVA and was not told to climb, by neither Person A nor myself. Aircraft X then requested higher as he was entering the 044 MVA, which then Person A told Aircraft X to contact ZZZ [ARTCC]. It was at that time I realized he wasnâ€™t told to climb to 090 and keyed up to have him climb, though I did not issue a Low Altitude Alert. He was 3 miles in the MVA at the time. We shouldâ€™ve put a focus on that aircraft and had continued their climb.

Synopsis.Narrative: TRACON Controller reported they forgot to inform an aircraft to climb before it flew below the MVA.

1.Text: Aircraft was in cruise flight, 34,000 ft., on a weather deviation approximately 35 miles east of route between the ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 intersections. Flight was proceeding normally; we were anticipating a turn back on course to rejoin before ZZZZZ2 (turning back approximately abeam position ZZZZZ1) as we tracked the weather via radar and satellite data from the Weather App. Aircraft was dispatched with 2 MELs â€“ 21-XX-XXX Packs and A46-YY-YYY Domestic Enroute (USA) CPDLC Restricted. The first MEL meant that we were operating with a single PACK â€“ #2. (Pack #1 was OFF per the procedure of the MEL.) Due to reported SatCom outages â€“ Dispatch just happened to choose our flight to do a SatCom voice check. As the non-normal unfolded this fortuitous SatCom call from the company helped expedite communications to prep ZZZZ Operations for the divert. We were able to communicate our intentions and had both dispatch and Maintenance Control looped in on the issue as it was happening live. We received the following ECAMs: Air Pack 1+2 Fault. CAB PR Lo Diff PR. CAB PR Excess Cab Alt. We followed SOP in accordance with an aeronautical decision-making model and worked the ECAMs as they presented themselves. I called for priority handling on 121.5 (guard) â€“ announced our intentions to divert to ZZZZ and we began an expedited descent to 10,000 ft. ZZZ [ARTCC] Air Traffic Control responded to our distress call â€“ gave us a new frequency, established radar contact, and gave us a vector towards the airport (ZZZZ). We donned our O2 masks and established flight deck communications. Continued to work the non-normal while on the expedited descent. The situation continued to evolve as the associated ECAMs began appearing â€“ i.e., CAB PR Lo Diff PR & CAB PR Excess Cab Alt. I communicated to inflight via the call button â€“ they answered right away. I told them that we were in a situation. Explained the reason (loss of pressurization system) and told them our time to landing. I also made a PA to the passengers letting them know that we would be making an unscheduled stop, giving them a non-technical explanation of the problem, and that weâ€™d have more information for them on the ground for how they would continue their journey to ZZZ. I was told during the post-flight debrief with the inflight crew that I did a stellar job pushing and pulling the information to both inflight and the passengers. Inflight felt very calm about the whole non-normal as it evolved. (Aside from the ear-popping) inflight told me that the passengers were very calm and nonplussed the whole time. My PA from the flight deck diffused any cabin stress that would have led to an undesirable outcome once on the ground. We continued working aspects of the non-normal and transited into the arrival and approach phase of the flight. Our new destination was inputted, weather obtained, approach was built and briefed, charts and airport company pages reviewed. In this phase of flight â€“ everything was stable. The cabin altitude was at a safe breathable level, we had removed our O2 masks and reestablished flight deck comms. Important to note, the passenger O2 masks DID NOT deploy from the Passenger Service Units (PSUs) during the non-normal. We were proceeding on a vector to our approach â€“ RVAV XX into ZZZZ. I took the time to review the Overweight Landing QRH Checklist. (Our landing weight was 147.8 â€“ a couple of thousand pounds higher than max for that particular weight variant.) Also, the divert checklist in the Manual. I wanted to ensure that we were covering all of our bases and not missing anything. I also reviewed the steps we took during the non-normal up to this point â€“ I â€œtalked out loudâ€ while FO and I discussed what got us from 34,000 ft. to this approach into ZZZZ and plainly asked, â€œDid we forget anything?â€ The aircraft was expertly landed in ZZZZ by FO. He followed the guidance in accordance with the overweight checklist. â€œSoftâ€ touchdown and the brakes did not heat up above approximately 200 C. We taxied to the gate where we were met by Station Operations, Local Crash Fire Rescue (CFR), Local Customs and Immigration, and Local Maintenance Control representatives. Times were noted and passed to dispatch. I made the following write-ups in the logbook: AIR Pack 1+2 Fault Inflight â€“ may have been due to OVHT condition. CAB PR Excess CAB ALT ECAM â€“ associated with the above write-up. CAB PR LO Diff PR â€“ associated with write-ups. Overweight landing due to divert â€“ Landing Weight: 147,800 lb., soft touchdown, temperatures less than 210 C. NAV Tuning LS Disagree Inflight â€“ reset as per QRH â€“ continued normally. The 5th write-up was not associated with the situation, non-normal, or divert. After that I talked with the Maintenance Control representative, Station Operations, and made a PA for the passengers talking about next steps. Passengers were deplaned and the non-normal was debriefed (informally) with all of the crew. Aircraft was taken out of service and a flight was dispatched. Any unintentional (or otherwise) deviations from SOP were done under Captainâ€™s Authority under the appropriate FARs. Any errors were trapped using our Threat and Error Management (TEM) model. I would like to commend (and sincerely thank) the crew â€“ FO and FAs â€“ for their professionalism and skill during the event and divert to ZZZZ. Their quick thinking, calm demeanor, and adherence to SOP made this a very easy problem to navigate. I may be the final authority and ultimately responsible for the flight, but we couldnâ€™t have done what we did without the support of the whole crew doing their jobs competently and without delay. They are all the best. Iâ€™d also like to thank the instructor pilots at Company. Every instructor that I interacted during every training event for the past years contributed to the safe outcome of this non-normal. In conclusion, we had a safe and successful outcome. I can tell you honestly that I will be debriefing this incident internally for the rest of my career â€“ with many lessons learned. Our flight had a serious mechanical problem and we stayed off social media and out of the news. The passengers seemed genuinely not annoyed with the outcome â€“ they still got to their final destination, albeit a little later than they hoped. Our training and the safety systems worked the way that they were designed. It wasnâ€™t perfect â€“ no real world non-normal is. Iâ€™m very proud of my crew and itâ€™s ultimately because of them (and the whole Company support structure) that we completed the flight as successfully as we did.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported diverting after the flight crew received several ECAMs of a cabin pressurization malfunction.

1.Text: On the descent to ZZZ at 16000 ft we started encountering moderate to severe turbulence that resulted in at least 500-800 ft and bank of over 20 degrees. It smoothed out after. However during the approach the plane lost GPS signal followed by loss of Auto thrust and auto pilot around 11000-10000 feet. It was followed by thrust lock. The captain took over manually and we were fully stable with the landing checklist done by 1000 RA and landed safely and uneventful.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 First Officer reported temporary loss of aircraft control due to turbulence.

1.Text: On Day 0, I was operating ZZZ1-ZZZ. On arrival, at approximately 16000ft, severe turbulence happened. Flight attendants and passengers were seated and no injuries happened. But about 500ft of altitude was lost and 20deg bank happened. Control was gained again of the aircraft on the arrival. But few minutes later on the approach, ecam for loss of automation, auto pilot and auto thrust, loss of gps and glideslope was giving wrong guideance. 1.Text: After a gate return the ramp informed us we needed to move the aircraft post deplaning in order to hook up external power. During pushback the aircraft became disconnected from the tug. At no time did the ground crew say "breakaway" they just said to set brakes. I gently applied brakes once I understood what was happening, took about a half a second to recognize the situation. Ramp found another tug and moved us into position.

1.Text: We were scheduled to operate from ZZZ-ZZZZ in an aircraft with an inoperative Hot Air Valve per MEL. After engine start the air conditioning system appeared to operate normally. We departed from runway XXR and passing 8000â€™ the inflight crew contacted the flight deck with a report that the air is blowing very loud, all passengers are turning off gaspers, the air is surging and there is a loud whistling sound. They indicated it was not normal and something was wrong. At the same time the cockpit became uncomfortably hot and the air was not blowing from any cockpit vents. I briefed my FO and we decided to level at 10000â€™ enter into holding and troubleshoot the issue, for concerns of pressurization. After transferring control and radios to the FO, the CA reviewed the system pages of the Bleed Air, which did not indicate any faults and reviewed the system pages of the Pressurization which did not indicate any faults. The CA then contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control and discussed the malfunction. Maintenance Control could not find any issues on their end, however we clearly had a malfunction on our end that was not producing any ECAM messages. After consulting with Dispatch and Maintenance Control I advised them that we felt taking an aircraft into mountainous terrain, would not be the safest course of action. They both supported my decision to return to ZZZ. All checklists and procedures were conducted at this time, including diversion and overweight landing checklist. The CA setup a return to ZZZ and throughly briefed the FO on our approach. The crew was briefed and passengers were advised. There were no issues with the return. Once we completed parking checklist the CA made a logbook entry for the malfunction and overweight landing. The Chief Pilot and Assistant Chief Pilot then made their way to the cockpit and asked for a detailed explanation of what occurred. A offline commercial pilot was in the cabin and commented as he deplaned that he knew that something was wrong with the system. We debriefed the inflight crew and they all heard the same loud noise, whistling, surging of air, and abnormal air pressure coming from the gaspers. We then debriefed with the Chief Pilots at the gate in the terminal.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported a malfunction with air conditioning system inflight. Flight returned to the departure airport and landed uneventfully.

1.Text: On flight to ZZZZ, we were departing on ZZZZZ departure out of ZZZ At 7000 feet and climbing, we had a VENT SKIN FAULT. We proceeded with the Non normal procedures. As per checklist we controlled this item. Following this item we had a AIR ENG 2 BLEED FAULT. We proceeded to do non normal procedures as per checklist, but did not reset. As we are getting this caution, we got the VENT BLOWER FAULT AND EXTRACT FAULT again. I called Fight attendant and explained the situation. At that time, we decided to hold on a fix. We called company, Maintenance Control and they recommended to reset items which did not reset. Passengers were calm and explained of the situation. I did call again to the flight attendants and we decided to call a briefing. The reason i did not continue was, because for safety of the flight and pressurization abnormalities. We secure items with non normal procedures and we did a overweight QRH procedure following the divert guide. We landed safely. Maintenance Control came to the plane and i wrote up items and overweight landing on a/c (Aircraft) book. We did not declare an emergency on that situation. Passengers were calm and transferred to another aircraft. Maintenance Control told us that this aircraft was having the same issues, but in different phases of flight. This happened and reported in other previous flights.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported multiple ECAM messages during climb. Flight returned to departure airport and landed safely.

1.Text: On preflight, it was discovered that the spinner faring on engine 1 had cracks/fractures around one of the bolt fastening locations. The first officer and myself were not comfortable, continuing with a compromised faring that is under extreme stress at the front of the engine that could lead to possible failure and ingestion.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported discovering engine issues during preflight, resulting in the Captain refusing the aircraft.

1.Text: On arrival into ZZZ, ZZZ Approach vectored us on a downwind for runway XX. Descending down to 4,000 we got a TA for GA traffic that was in sight and pointed out to us by approach. We then received an RA as it looked like he was climbing within 500 feet of us as we passed over. I disconnected autopilot, flew into the green [band] and climbed no higher than 4,300 feet before clear of conflict. Engaged automation and continued the arrival after notifying approach. Cause: GA traffic wasn't in contact with approach as he was under the shelf. The only mitigation would be to maybe have leveled off at a higher altitude, but overall I believe all parties did what they should have, it was just an unusual case of GA traffic flying near a downwind without communication.

2.Text: Descending in the terminal area near ZZZ, ATC alerted us to VFR traffic below us at 12 to 1 o'clock position. We identified the traffic on TCAS then acquired the traffic visually. We were cleared to 4,000 MSL and the target traffic was at 3,500 MSL. Approaching 4,500 ft we received a TA. At approximately 4,100 ft it upgraded to an RA with a "Level Off" guidance. The FO (PF) accomplished the RA procedure per the AOM and leveled at 4,100. Cause: TCAS gave an Resolution Advisory due to the altitude approaching 500 ft separation although both us and the VFR traffic remained at assigned altitudes.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 flight crew reported receiving a TA and RA.

1.Text: During a night visual approach to runway XXR in ZZZ with the first officer flying while I monitored, we received a low altitude alert from ATC and elected to abandon the approach and try again. We were initially expecting runway XXR, but when the ATIS was advertising that runway XYL was in use, we changed the approach in the FMS and briefed for runway XYL. Upon contacting approach control, the controller advised that the winds were from the south and gave us the option of XZ or XXR. We chose XXR, due to the runway being longer, and a runway assessment indicated we had adequate runway to land with a slight tailwind. As we descended to 2000 feet for the approach, we picked up the runway visually and were cleared for a visual approach. The final approach fix altitude was 1600 feet, and the first officer selected 1600 as the next altitude while arming the ILS XXR approach. However, when the autopilot captured the ILS signal, it turned away from the runway and paralleled the course instead. It was then that I realized that the ILS signal must have still been set to runway XYL. The ILS frequency for both XXR and XYL were the same, and I had not seen the IDENT displayed on the Primary Flight Display (PFD). The other issue was that the PAPI for that runway was out of service, so it was difficult to determine our glide path. The first officer disconnected the autopilot and tried to return the aircraft to the centerline while I disengaged the flight directors. While I was trying to find an RNAV approach to quickly load into the FMS, ATC alerted us to our low altitude, and I saw we were at 1000 feet and still outside the final approach fix. We attempted to regain altitude to salvage the approach, but ATC offered to vector us back for another approach, and we agreed. At this point, we had already been configuring for landing, and we had the gear down and the flaps were at config 3. As we continued to climb, we were slow to reconfigure, and the aircraft was still at approach speed (160-170 knots) when I instructed the first officer to select TOGA, and we were finally able to climb to 2000 feet and reconfigure the aircraft. On the next approach, I noted the correct IDENT on the PDF for runway XXR, and we were able to successfully land. In hindsight, I should have known something was wrong with the ILS signal when I did not see the IDENT displayed. I also should have been monitoring the approach better and corrected the altitude deviation sooner, or at least commanded a full go-around once ATC alerted us. Cause: It has been many years since Iâ€™ve seen a situation where the ILS frequency is the same for both runways. I did not consider that multiple runways changes might cause the wrong runway to be selected by ATC, and I should have confirmed the correct IDENT before allowing the FO to arm the approach.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air carrier Captain reported low altitude alert was issued by ATC during a visual approach.

1.Text: Low speed RTO (Rejected Takeoff) due to significant asymmetric thrust during thrust application.. Aircraft speed was below 60 kts. ENG 1 appeared to have spooled normally but ENG 2 very little if any sign of spooling. Flight returned to the gate for maintenance action

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 pilot reported significant asymmetric thrust during takeoff roll resulting in a rejected takeoff.

1.Text: We departed the gate and had a quick taxi to XXL @ Taxiway 1. The takeoff was a normal with a strong crosswind from the south. After takeoff (Approx. 1000ft) an ECAM appeared. HYD Y RSVR LO LVL followed by I believe a PTU (Power Transfer Unit) Fault and a low pressure. We told departure that we needed to stop the climb and take care of an issue. At this time we had not declared an emergency. We leveled at 5000ft, maintained 220 kts, on a heading of 270, and the autopilot was ON. The ECAM was announce and we decided that I would continue flying and the PM would run the ECAM. The PM went through the items instructed by the ECAM. I was flying and working the radios, but I believe the PTU was turned off and possibly the yellow engine pump. After the ECAM was completed and the screens were normal, the PM contacted dispatch via ACARS and was given a frequency so that we could have verbal communication. According to the PM communication was difficult due to poor reception. After we discussed the situation, we decided that returning to ZZZ was the best option. We discussed requesting priority handling and decide to do so because of the spoilers 2 and 4 being inop. After our plans were settled I requested priority handling and notified ATC of our intentions, souls, and fuel on board. ATC began vectoring us for an ILS to XYC. The PM informed the FA of the situation and gave them a briefing. Dispatch sent us landing distance numbers approx, 8900 feet which was well within the 10800 feet for XYC. The PM ran through the Overweight Landing Checklist. I configured early and dropped the gear early to burn more fuel to reduce the overweight landing issue, and the flaps would be moving slower than normal. The autopilot came off at about 1000 feet. The flight controls felt spongier than normal but not so much that aircraft was difficult to control. The strong crosswind remained present. I would consider the touchdown to be smooth. The Capt took the controls at 80 knots and taxied off the runway at Taxiway 2 and held on taxiway 3 short of 4. Emergency vehicles were behind us. We went to frequency XXX.XX where ground and emergency services were accessible. Emergency service circled the aircraft and found no evidence of damage or fire. The brakes topped out at 505C on the number 1 caliper. The other were 380 to 425. We discussed our ability to taxi in but were hesitant due to the brake temp and we had been made aware that a fluid was now leaking from the belly of the aircraft. A tug arrived and we decided out of an abundance of caution that we would be towed in. This took a while. Mx (Maintenance) arrived and asked for the gear pins. We had trouble locating the gear pins. They asked if the aircraft taxied fine. We stated yes and since the brakes had cooled significantly, we decided to taxi it back to the gate. The aircraft was choked at the gate and the maintenance requests were sent in.

2.Text: Departing ZZZ on our third flight to ZZZ1, climbing out of 1000 feet we had yellow hydraulic reservoir low ECAM. Additional messages came up with that failure. I was the pilot monitoring, and I informed ATC that we needed too level off at 5000 feet to work a problem. I asked the FO if he was comfortable flying and working the radios so I could run the checklist, and he was. He turned on the autopilot and continue to fly and work the radios. We ran through the procedure together, verifying everything was done correctly. At that point I tried a call me message for a frequency with dispatch and Maintenance Control. Since we were at 5000 feet, we had a hard time hearing dispatch and I've ended up telling them our plan was to return to ZZZ, the dispatcher was phenomenal and getting us landing data and information we needed for landing. We advised ATC. We set up for a return to ZZZ and briefed the plan. I then called the flight attendants and advised them of the situation as well as notified the passengers. We were aware of the possibility of an overweight landing and had a discussion on burning the fuel or just going into land. We elected to land as we were down one hydraulic system. The landing was incredibly smooth and uneventful. Being that we were overweight and heavy, we had the fire trucks meet the airplane as a precautionary measure. Once off the runway, the fire trucks notified us that we did have hydraulic fluid leaking out of the belly, it was described as a slow drip. I communicated with dispatch and Maintenance Control on the ground for the safest course of action with hot brakes. I'm not sure who, but somebody sent us a tug so we thought we would use the tug to get back to the gate. Unfortunately, in the midst of the chaos, I could not find the gear pins in the flight deck as that back closet was dark and the gear pin holder was a dark color. This is no way in excuse that I could not find them, just telling you the real time situation as I was trying to communicate with everybody and find gear pins for the tug in. At this point, the brakes had cooled down enough that we discussed with maintenance and they thought it would be better if we could just taxi in so that's what we elected to do. (once maintenance arrived at the airplane. We did shut the engines down in preparation for being towed in). We started the engines back up and order a taxi back to the gate uneventfully. We coordinated with operations to chock us ASAP as the checklist says that the brake accumulator may not hold the aircraft in position. Maintenance personnel met us at the gate where we continued the discussion of what happened.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 flight crew reported loss of a hydraulic system during climb phase. Crew returned to departure airport.

1.Text: We were #1 for departure and holding short in ZZZ when we noticed ENG2 TLA FAULT on ECAM. As I was preparing to call Maintenance control, we selected status page and message went away and the Navigation Display had nothing except NORMAL indication. We cleared status page and ECAM no longer appeared and TO CONFIGURATION PAGE was present where all green no blue was present. No STS white flag was present and we selected status page to verify one last time and there were no indications of abnormalities. Page was cleared and All was normal. We decided message cleared itself and there was no longer a need to contact Maintenance control. We proceeded with a TOGA TO and all went normal. After takeoff from ZZZ, at 2000ft after flap retraction we had en Eng2 THR LVR disagree ECAM. We complied with ECAM ACTIONS QRH. Also Sat Com with dispatch, Mx was performed. Requested priority handling with ATC and a FAs were briefed. We continued to ZZZ1 as we were 10 minutes away. We landed with Eng 2 Thr at idle per the QRH and proceeded to gate where a normal deplaning occurred. Mx write-ups were performed.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 pilot reported a ENG 2 thrust lever angle ECAM warning on climb. Crew continued to destination and landed with the engine operating at idle thrust.

1.Text: During pushback I notified the push crew first to â€œstandby,â€ then when cleared by ramp I said â€œcleared to push tail northâ€. I did not release the brake and I failed to say â€œbrakes released.â€ An unusual sound was heard and I immediately realized that the brake was still set. The push crew stopped the push and investigated for any damage - I informed him that the brake had not been released. They advised that tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. I released the brake and the push continued. About 50 yards into the push the crew stopped and had me set brakes. Something was not right with the tow bar and they had to swap it out. Once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push. Nearing the desired drop point, the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as I waited for the driver to advise me to â€œset brakes.â€ Just then the tug and the aircraft began to roll forward and the driver said â€œCaptain brakes brakes.â€ I immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes and stated â€œbrakes set, cleared to disconnect inter phone.â€ I had assumed the aircraft was still being positioned by the tug driver, but perhaps we had been disconnected without brakes being set. On taxiout we entered the hardstand. The FO researched tow bar pin shear (FOM requires inspection) as we both began to wonder if that may have occurred. Since we were off gate we contacted Dispatch and were patched through to Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control did great work to coordinate with ZZZ Maintenance and OPs to find out if there was a shear. While we waited in the hardstand the FO and I decided it best to taxi back to gate and get the nose gear inspected just in case there was a pin shear. We taxied back to Gate XX, shutdown and entered an logbook entry. There was notably good collaboration at the gate from our Maintenance team including the original ground crew providing their inputs so that the inspection could be done properly. With the inspection complete we departed without further issue. Cause: Causal was my failure to release the parking brake prior to authorizing the push. My normal habit is to say â€œstandbyâ€ after receiving the guide personâ€™s â€œall secure belowâ€ advisory, which I did. But when I reviewed the ECAM just prior to clearing the pushback I only noted the NW STRG DISC memo and failed to note the Park Brake memo. And I didnâ€™t state â€œBrakes releasedâ€ nor did I release the brakes. I am going to add a technique of pointing to the parking brake handle and then to the ECAM prior to stating â€œbrakes released, cleared to push.â€ This was suggested by the FO who has seen other CAs using this technique. And while I didnâ€™t feel rushed, I think making this process a slower and more deliberate execution will do me well in the future. Iâ€™m certain that the drop point rolling issue was part of this cascade from the non standard pushback. The guide person was very quick to catch the issue and call for brakes.

2.Text: We were given the brief from the pushback crew but had not completed our Before Start Checklist and had not received our pushback clearance from ramp. The Captain told the push crew to â€œstandby.â€ Then once we were cleared by ramp to push he informed the ramp crew â€œcleared to push tail northâ€. At that point the parking brake was still set. (Normal call â€œbrakes released, cleared to push (tail north)â€). When the ramp crew went to push we heard an unusual noise. Then we realized that the parking brake had not been released. The Captain then notified the ramp crew to stop the push and investigate for any damage. Additionally, he informed him that the parking brake had not been released. After the ramp crew investigated, they advised us that the tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. The captain released the brake and the push continued. After about 50 yards, the push the crew stopped and had us set brakes. They informed us that there was an issue with the tow bar and it needed to be swapped out. Once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push. Nearing the desired drop point, the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as the captain waited for the driver to advise â€œset brakes.â€ We then noticed the tug driving away and the aircraft appeared to be rolling forward. Shortly after this the driver said â€œCaptain brakes brakes.â€ The Captain immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes. Then he notified them that the brakes were set and they were cleared to disconnect the interphone. To us what had appeared to have happened was the aircraft was still being pulled by the tug driver, but other indications made us question what was happening. I believe the tug driver was a little shaken from the previous events that had occurred but the error had been trapped and damage/injury was prevented.. On taxiout, I researched the publications for tow bar issues and discovered we may have sheared a tow pin and needed an inspection. We coordinated with ramp to hold in the hard stand and worked with Dispatch, Maintenance Control, ZZZ Ops, ZZZ maintenance, and ramp to setup an inspection. We proceeded to a new gate for the inspection. The Captain made an logbook entry and maintenance performed the inspection. We then proceed with the flight with no further issues and as a crew talked about what had happened and ways to prevent such a miscommunication in the future. Cause: The cause of the event was a miscommunication between the Captain and the push crew. He did inform them that we were cleared to push but never said that the brakes were released. I can see why this was confusing for the push crew. Depending on the situation, Captains sometimes release the parking brake immediately after the brief is received from the push crew but tells the push crew to standby for the push clearance. Also Iâ€™m curious how often the push crews ensure the light is out prior to initiating the push. If the push crew would have referenced the light this would have been trapped and no error would have occurred.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air carrier flight crew reported non compliant push back verbiage resulting in nose wheel shear pin damage. Lack of communication then resulted in the aircraft rolling forward because the "set brakes" command was never given.

1.Text: While descending to cross ZZZZZ at 12,000 feet, we received a ECAM message indicating the loss of the blue hydraulic system. The Captain immediately established clear task division, assigning me the flying pilot and radios while he focused on ECAM actions and system management. This early role clarification ensured effective workload distribution and situational awareness. At the time of the event, we were still some distance from ZZZ. The Captain elected to continue briefly on the cleared path to assess whether sufficient time was available to properly run the ECAM procedures and associated non-normal checklists without rushing. This decision allowed us to maintain control of the situation in a measured and deliberate manner. ATC provided early speed reduction, which helped create additional time and space to manage the situation. Communication between the Captain and Dispatch was timely, clear, and effective, contributing positively to our decision-making process. Crew coordination throughout the event was strong. We maintained continuous cross-checking and open communication, ensuring both pilots remained aligned on aircraft status, intentions, and next steps. The CRM demonstrated during this event was effective and supportive, with both pilots actively monitoring and assisting each other. After completing the required non-normal procedures and requesting priority handling, we jointly decided to continue the approach and land at the destination. Following touchdown, we brought the aircraft to a stop on the runway to assess for any additional issues before proceeding. Emergency services, ATC, and Dispatch were all engaged and supportive. No further abnormalities were identified, and the remainder of the operation was uneventful. We subsequently taxied back to the gate and conducted a thorough post-flight debrief.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 First Officer reported a hydraulic system malfunction during the descent. The flight continued to the destination and landed.

1.Text: During my cockpit preparation, when testing my oxygen mask the pressure dropped rapidly from 1,200psi to less than 900psi. The amount of pressure lost was not normal to me so I had the first officer test his again with the same result. When the First Officer and I tested our oxygen together, the pressure dropped from 1,200psi to zero within seconds. A logbook entry was made, and upon inspection by the Maintenance Business Partner they found that the crew oxygen bottle was CLOSED. This is NOT the first time this has occurred.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported failure of the oxygen system test during pre-flight at the gate. Maintenance inspection revealed the bottle valve was fully closed.

1.Text: Immediately after starting descent from FL340 multiple ECAMS illuminated: ENG 2 EPR MODE FAULT N1 DEGRADED MODE along with AUTO FLT A/THR OFF. We had a third ECAM but I can't remember what it was. We lost #2 EGT and Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR). We executed the QRC and then proceeded with the ECAM action. I immediately formulated a plan to not go to ZZZ1 due to the #2 thrust reverser being inop coupled with a short runway, the current EPR issue and fuel possibly becoming an issue, I communicated this with the FO for his input and he concurred, so I coordinated with ATC and asked for holding at FL300 to give more time to work the issue. I was the pilot flying and the FO was monitoring so we maintained those positions for the remainder of the flight. After finishing ECAM actions I had the FO go to the follow up items as I continued to fly and communicate to ATC. After a brief discussion with the FO I favored the notifying ATC option and communicated that with ATC followed with Souls on Board and 1.5 hours of fuel. We did three turns in holding which allowed for us to finish everything we needed to do inside and outside the aircraft to include the comms to dispatch, FAs, the passengers and ZZZ ops to make sure they were ready for us. We setup the arrival and approach and slowly worked towards ZZZ. We completed all checklists and landed without incident. Tower wasn't sure as to our plan for leaving the runway after landing so we told them we would clear immediately after landing. Fire trucks still responded even though they weren't requested, followed us to the gate and we shutdown the engines. The FO and I did a post flight inspection walk around of the aircraft specifically the right engine and saw no anomalies. I communicated with chief pilot who passed on the info to the IOC Duty pilot, dispatch informing them the plane was grounded awaiting contract maintenance, and Maintenance Control due to the out of base write up. The FO did a great job of remaining calm and helping me work the issue. His input and dedication to the task at hand was perfect and the interaction between us was seamless. SIDE NOTE: Major issue with the wording on the ECAM vs what's on the switch- wording is mismatched which caused an unnecessary distraction and wasted time in proceeding to the 2nd ECAM which was turning off AUTOTHRUST, which almost led to an MMO overspeed. The ECAM says: ENG 2 N1 MODE ON ENG 1 N1 MODE ON While we presumed this was actually the Full Authority Digital Engine Control (FADEC)s it doesn't say that and I was concerned about the result of turning them on during flight (it's labeled GROUND POWER and a guarded switch for a reason?!) and possibly exacerbating this issue or creating another issue. So I had the FO scrub the manual to confirm that N1 MODE= FADEC during holding in an attempt to complete the first ECAM action. Meanwhile the airspeed was slowly creeping up as we delayed doing the third item of the 1st ECAM - move the thrust levers, since we hadnâ€™t resolved the 1st two items of the first ECAM . This distraction brought us real close to an MMO overspeed but I caught it prior to it occurring. I retarded the thrust levers appropriate to the speed needed. We then circled back to the 1st two items of the first ECAM and the search for N1 MODE. Cause: there seems to be a mismatch of ECAM procedures and the name of the switch which should be looked into further.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported multiple ECAM indications during cruise. Flight diverted and landed without incident.

1.Text: Our flight was from ZZZ. We boarded Aircraft X and found the flight deck and forward galley in a bit of disarray, with gear pins, papers, and rags on the cockpit floor and a mechanicâ€™s headset and pitot tube covers in the galley. The aircraft had been sitting in ZZZ for what I recall was a few days from the logbook. We requested that a mechanic come to retrieve any items that didnâ€™t belong on the airplane and ensure that everything that was required to be onboard was accounted for, which they did. My FO verified that no gear-pins, collars, reverser locking pins, etc. were in place on the exterior of the aircraft. We departed on time and taxied to runway XXL for takeoff. The takeoff was normal and we received a vector of 230 and clearance to 10,000 feet from ZZZ departure. Passing through approximately 6,000 feet, an ECAM message appeared, â€œENG 2 EGT OVER-TEMPâ€ with engine parameters in agreement. I was the pilot monitoring and began the non-normal plan strategy, which led us to reducing thrust to see if the EGT would come below the high-limit. It did, but after a brief discussion of our situation and about how such a reduction in thrust didnâ€™t make flying all the way to our destination seem very practical or wise, we decided that returning to ZZZ would be prudent. This discussion was cut short by a second ECAM, â€œENG2 EPR MODE FAILâ€, so the plan strategy began once again. The ECAM action led us to a reversion to N1 mode of thrust control and subsequent loss of auto-thrust, and that went smoothly. My FO, whose capacity to fly the aircraft extraordinarily well and handle high task-loading with apparent ease (while I was quite busy with QRH followups, STATUS page updates, the ECAM Supplemental manual, diversion notification, etc.), was able to observe that increasing the thrust on the affected engine close to climb would cause another over temperature condition while decreasing the thrust to idle also caused a sharp increase in temperature up to the limit. Unusual. I notified the flight attendants and passengers of the need to return to ZZZ for a mechanical discrepancy. We notified ATC for a more immediate return to the airport; although the situation was quite under control, the strange behavior of the EGT on the affected engine gave us enough reason to think being on the ground sooner than later would be a good idea. We performed an overweight landing checklist for what would be a landing at approximately 4,000 pounds over maximum landing weight. During landing the #2 engine thrust reverser didnâ€™t deploy, and displayed amber when selected to reverse. After clearing the runway we noticed that the #2 engine, when at idle, was approximately 150 degrees hotter than the #1 engine at idle, but within limits. After shutdown, we also noted an â€œENG2 FADECâ€ Class 2 status message. Before I had the chance to pick up my iPad to begin making all of the necessary logbook entries, we were greeted on the flight deck by two mechanics who noted that they werenâ€™t very surprised by our return because the airplane had â€œquite a historyâ€. They mentioned that the work done on the airplane over the last day or two involved replacing pieces of a wiring harness, but the reality was that the airplane simply needed an engine change. I canâ€™t speak to the veracity of that statement, but it was said to me. I spoke with our dispatcher, Chief Pilot. We swapped to another A-320 at the neighboring gate and departed about 2 hours late for a successful flight. Cause: The specific causal factors, at least in so far as what caused the EGT to over-temp in such a way with the follow-on failures (Engine Pressure Ratio mode failure, thrust reverser failure, Full Authority Digital Engine Control fault) aren't available to me at this point, so I could only speculate. My decades of experience flying turbine engines would lead me to believe that the engine's turbine tolerances had become excessive and the engine was simply out of time. That would agree with the statement the mechanics made to me, but I can't verify that. As I sit writing this, it's not immediately apparent to me why an EGT exceedance (at least one that's not severe) would cause the other issues, too. Concerning this, I don't have any recommendations for this situation to be prevented, but I can speak to the effectiveness of the planned strategy and of course recommend the reinforcement of its teaching. An EGT over-temp on a high-time engine for a brief period during takeoff isn't exactly unheard of, and in fact is even allowed in some cases with a maintenance discrepancy item, but this event unfolded in a rather unexpected way after the over-temp occurred, and the planned strategy is indispensable in such a situation.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported returning to departure airport after experiencing an engine EGT over-temp on climb out.

1.Text: Shortly after departure from ZZZ Airport, while climbing through approximately 1,500 feet AGL, the crew received an amber ECAM message: DOOR R AFT EMERGENCY EXIT. The message appeared after the Takeoff Inhibit phase, at which point we leveled at 5,000 feet and requested vectors to troubleshoot. ECAM and QRH procedures were initiated. Per QRH guidance, continuation of flight may be considered if pressurization is confirmed normal. However, during coordination with the cabin crew, a physical inspection of the door revealed that the handle had become detached and the door appeared unsecured (â€œunlockedâ€/not properly seated). This created a discrepancy between: System indications and QRH conditional guidance, and Direct physical observation from the cabin crew indicating a potential door integrity issue. Additionally, due to the early phase of flight in which the ECAM message occurred (approximately 1,500 feet AGL), there was limited opportunity to reliably assess cabin pressurization performance prior to reaching higher altitudes where any degradation could become operationally significant. Given: The uncertainty regarding the mechanical status of the emergency exit, The abnormal condition of a detached handle, The limited ability to confirm stable pressurization early in the climb, The planned routing over the ZZZZZ/oceanic segment, where diversion options are more limited, I assessed that continuing the flight would introduce unnecessary risk, particularly in the event of a pressurization or structural issue. Given these factors, delaying the decision until further climb would have reduced available margins and increased exposure to risk in a less favorable operational environment. After completing the QRH, I coordinated with Dispatch via SATCOM, briefed the passengers, and elected to return to ZZZ for a precautionary landing. The aircraft landed without further incident.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain on initial climb reported the handle broke off the rear door and it did not seal properly so they returned to departure airport.

1.Text: I was assigned from reserve to operate Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1. During preflight, the First Officer and I reviewed the aircraft logbook and MELs. Multiple MELs were noted, including two related to the air conditioning system. Neither MEL contained Operations Procedures or notes indicating degraded cabin temperature performance. During cockpit preparation, I observed the PACK FLOW selector in the HIGH position. As this was not required by any MEL or procedure, it was returned to NORM. Pushback was slightly delayed due to ramp congestion. Taxi and takeoff were uneventful. During climb, passing approximately 10,000 feet, the flight attendants reported increasing cabin temperatures in the aft cabin. In response, I selected all temperature zones to full cold and set PACK FLOW to HIGH. A subsequent report from the cabin indicated that conditions were worsening, with very hot air from the vents. The COND page was reviewed and indicated increasing cabin temperatures and elevated trim air temperature (approximately 150°C). I made a PA to inform passengers that we were working to address the situation. At that point, I transferred aircraft control to the First Officer and requested a level-off from ATC to allow time for system evaluation and troubleshooting. No ECAM messages were present, and no applicable non-annunciated procedures were identified in the QRH. Based on system indications, we selected the HOT AIR pushbutton OFF; no improvement was observed. I established communication with Maintenance Control via SATCOM and provided a summary of system indications and cabin reports. In coordination with Maintenance Control, we selected the HOT AIR push button OFF and performed a pack reset. These actions did not result in any sustained improvement. Cabin temperatures continued to increase, reaching approximately 105°F forward and 100°F aft. Concurrently, the cabin crew continued to report worsening conditions and increasing passenger discomfort. Given the lack of response to corrective actions, continued adverse temperature indications, and ongoing cabin reports, the First Officer and I assessed the situation as a safety concern and elected to discontinue the flight and return to ZZZ. The First Officer coordinated the return with ATC while I remained in communication with Maintenance Control. During the return, trim air temperature briefly decreased; however, cabin temperatures remained elevated and subsequently increased again. Based on this trend, the decision to return was reaffirmed. I advised the cabin crew and passengers of the return. Due to workload during the approach phase, I contacted ZZZ operations via VHF to advise of the return and request notification to dispatch. The approach and landing were uneventful. After arrival at the gate, a logbook entry was made and the aircraft was subsequently removed from service.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported air conditioning system issues resulting in very high ambient temperatures and return to departure airport.

1.Text: The flight crew arrived at ZZZZ to operate Aircraft X to ZZZ1 on-time on Day 0. While completing our receiving checklist, the CA noticed that the CA's oxygen mask (interphone) would not test properly, and that there was not a proper "switch over," to the mask-microphone function. After confirming that the First Officer's mask was working properly, and attempting to resolve the issue multiple times, dispatch was informed and maintenance was called to the aicraft. Maintenance confirmed that the CA's mask was not working properly, and upon further investgiation, damage was found to the cables connecting the mask to the aicraft in the flight deck. Maintenance informed us that they would "swap," the mask assembly box with the second observer's mask to resolve the issue. This process took several hours as it proved to be a difficult task to accomplish due to the ergonomics of the assemblies. After the procedure was complete, the maintenance technicians proceeded to begin the "sign off," process, and took the logbook to "close out," the open write-up. While this was happening, the aircraft unexpectedly rolled forward completely uncommanded into the chocks. The Captain first noticed this, and it was confirmed by the remaining maintenance crew still onboard the aicraft. We verified that the parking brake was still engaged by first looking at the E/WD, and then looked at the "triple indicator," to see that both the accumulator and both brake pressure indicators were showing zero pressure. After coordinating with maintenance, the yellow pump was turned on which immediately pressurized the yellow system. Hydraulic cavitations were felt and heard, and the "triple indicator," immediatley showed tha the system was pressurized. At this point, we realized that there may be an issue with the accumulator. At no point did we suspect that the indicator was incorrectly reporting the pressure, as it was confirmed on two separate "known states," that the pressure was first "lost," and then "recharged." During the next 35-40 minutes of troubleshooting and invesgitation, we noticed that the presure in the accumulator was dropping rapidly, and the brake pressure indicators were also showing a loss of pressure. The manual states that "EFFECTIVE ON A/C ALL - Accumulators maintain the parking pressure for at least 12 hours. Yellow accumulators can be pressurized by pressuring the yellow electric pump switch. Brake and accumulator pressure are indiciated on the triple indicator." The total time elapsed from first parking brake application (aircraft block-in from ZZZ1) to the aircraft moving into the chocks was approxmately 3 hours -- clearly outside of the normal expectation for the system. At this point, we were notified that the airport authority had instructed us to move the aicraft off of the gate because it was needed for another aircraft. We proceeded to "deplane," the customers, and maintenance moved the aicraft to another suitable gate. This process took several hours, and during this time, on-site maintenance worked to test the aicraft and seek a resolution. Ultimately, the flight was cancelled due to the extended delay as the inflight crew had worked the incoming flight from ZZZ1, and we were rapidly approaching our MOT (Minimum Off Time). We were notified that we would be operating an extra section for the route, Aircraft Y on Day 1. The next morning, after waking up in ZZZZ, I noticed that the schedule stated that the flight would be operated with the same tail number, Aircraft X and there was an MEL applied -- MEL 32-XX-XXX. In my opinion, after reviewing the MEL details, this was an incorrect MEL for the situation, instead referencing the indicator not being correct. At this time, I felt that maintenance control was attempting to apply the MEL that would allow us to depart while the aicraft was still in an unsafe condition to fly. Ultimately, the issue was resolved via a "tail swap," to another aicraft, and Aircraft X was grounded.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 pilot reported parking brake pressure lost and aircraft rolled forward uncommanded into the chocks.

1.Text: While on RNP XX, ATC gave instruction to descend visually to 2900 MSL on RNP XX. We were in open descent mode on the approach. After being cleared for the approach, we set 2000 feet as the FAF altitude on the Flight Control Unit (FCU). While starting down visually and noticed we were in open descent mode. We were fully aware of nearby terrain and closure rate. The airplane warned of terrain closure, and PF arrested descent. This caused a flap overspeed that was immediately corrected by disconnecting AP and autothrust. The aircraft leveled off and continued the approach to an uneventful landing.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 First Officer reported the flight crew realized the FMA was in the wrong mode and received a terrain warning, leveled off which caused a flap overspeed, and then corrected the path to an uneventful landing.

1.Text: In VFR conditions on approach to [Runway] XX. ATC asked if we had visual on terrain, we said yes and proceeded to descend to 2900 and subsequently were cleared approach. We armed approach and set FAF in window. As we started down visually we realized our Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) was in open descent instead of descent mode. Aircraft warned of terrain and I allowed the airspeed to creep up from 180 flaps 2 to 200 while itâ€™s fixing descent issue. Leveled off, corrected the path and made an uneventful landing.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported the flight crew realized the FMA was in the wrong mode and received a terrain warning, leveled off which caused a flap overspeed, and then corrected the path to an uneventful landing.

1.Text: Take off and departure out of ZZZ1 was uneventful. We were filed at FL330, however there was continuous light turbulence so we opted to climb to FL350. Once getting to cruise, the crew completed the cruise checklist and there was nothing notable. About 20 minutes later (over ZZZ), we received the ECAM: HYD G RSVR LO LVL and HYD G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR and G SYS LO PR. The captain gave the controls and radios to me and started working through the ECAM. We discussed the failure as well as the status page before stating â€œECAM complete screens normalâ€. Once the ECAM was complete, we used radio to contact dispatch to determine our best course of action. With this failure needing a landing gear gravity extension and with ZZZ2 being a special qualification airport, we decided we didn't want to continue to our destination in case of executing a missed approach, where the gear would be left out and would make our climb more difficult in a mountainous terrain environment. At this point, we had 18,300 lbs of fuel remaining, which was plenty for any of those diversion options. Dispatch and Maintenance Control recommended to return back to ZZZ1. We notified ATC and returned back to ZZZ1 with vectors direct to the airport. We set up and briefed the approach, reviewed the landing gear gravity extension procedure, as well as the towing procedure. With the failure of the G HYD system, we had to stop on the runway (XXR) due to no Nose Wheel Steering. Airport Rescue and Firefighting was standing by and cleared the aircraft of any imminent threat. The tow was hooked up on the runway after completing the towing procedure checklist and we were towed back to gate XX.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 First Officer reported loss of the G hydraulic system at FL350 resulted in return to departure airport.

1.Text: Normal climb out of ZZZ1. Kept the flight attendants seated a little longer for turbulence. Finally found some smooth air and let everyone up. We had done our cruise checks and all systems looked normal. Was in cruise flight nearly an hour into the flight when we got an ECAM for HYD G SYS LO PR, G RSVR LO LVL, G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR. The hydraulic system page showed no fluid in the Green system. We followed the ECAM. We referenced the Flight Manual (FM). We alerted dispatch and the FA's. We talked to operations about best divert options. I didn't want to attempt a landing in ZZZ2 because we would be a fixed gear aircraft in the event of a go-around and the mountains and night time special airport was a concern. We talked about ZZZ3, ZZZ and ZZZ1. Operations said that ZZZ1 would be best for the operation. The FO and I discussed that if any other systems degraded we would drop immediately back to ZZZ but we felt ok to return to ZZZ1 for the best resources. We did a brief with the FA's but elected not to brace and no evacuation planned. We told the passengers the plan. We requested priority handling and returned to ZZZ1. Descent was normal. We asked ATC for a 20 mile final for XXR so we could do the gravity extension. All went according to plan. Landed, only 1 reverser but stopped using alternate braking. Set the parking brake, APU on, engines off. Airport Rescue and Firefighting checked us out. Brake temps were just under 500C on the left side and cooler on the right. Tow team came out quickly. We did the tow-in checklist. Advised all parties. Towed into Gate XX and it took us about 40 minutes to get to the gate. Per the Electronic Log Book, Maintenance found a blown out hydraulic supply line near the ENGINE 1 pylon.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported a hydraulic quantity malfunction during cruise. The flight returned to the departure airport, landed, and required a tow to the gate where maintenance found a leaking hydraulic line.

1.Text: Shortly after climbout and reaching cruise phase of flight out of ZZZ, experienced an amber ecam CAB PR 1. Ran ecam which were all advisory messages along with qrh, determined cabin pressure 1 was inop but sys 2 was holding. Would have been fine to continue on the leg if this was the case, but shortly after amber ecam cab pr 1, associated with this we experienced a red ecam of CAB PR Excess Cabin Alt. Obviously this was in error as we were holding can pressure within normal limits with normal delta Pressure, the problem we faced was the constant audible and visual warning in the main cabin where the customers/passengers were experiencing every time this ecam occurred on the Flt deck. This occurred a total of 4 times. In the interest of safety and passenger comfort and safety, I decided to precautionary Return to Base back to ZZZ, after completing a SAT call to discuss with maintenance and dispatch. Emergency was not declared not to add to the unusual circumstances and conditions we were facing, and sys 2 pressure held normal. Again the aural and emergency light visual indications in the main cabin along with the ecam warning messages deemed necessary to accomplish an air return, along with the possibility of sys 2 failing where we would have had no choice but to declare an emergency and execute rapid descent on our 2.5 hr flight.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 pilot reported a Pressurization System 1 malfunction while leveling at cruise altitude resulting in intermittent cabin warnings while the backup pressurization system maintained cabin pressure with system 2. Due to the intermittent audible and visual warnings, the flight returned to the departure airport.

1.Text: Due to the busy time frame in the late afternoon, ZZZZ tower was issuing line up and wait behind clearances for arriving and departing traffic. After crossing runway XX on taxiway 1, which was closed and not in use, we were instructed by ZZZZ tower to run numbers for taxiway 2 intersection departure for runway XY. We also asked about our sequence to the runway due to enroute spacing over the departure fixes mentioned to us while getting our clearance at the gate, and was told we were "behind an aircraft." After receiving this information, EFB returned good performance numbers for our intersection and the FO went through the departure changes checklist. After several inbound arrivals landed, we were now sequenced in front of said 737 who was holding short of runway XY full length from taxiway 1, while Aircraft X, another 737, was given a line up and wait for runway -full length. As we approached the runway XY/2 hold short line we were instructed to line up and wait. My FO read back the clearance "Aircraft X, runway XY, line up and wait" and I realized this would put us in front of the Aircraft Y 737 in position, but still give us adequate separation on the runway. He remarked to me "I guess weâ€™re going to cut him off" and I said, "yeah this is definitely a new one for me." While we were speaking to each other about the odd nuances of this scenario, ZZZ tower issued, in Spanish - what we can now later assume - a takeoff clearance to Aircraft Y. I continued to very slowly taxi the aircraft towards the hold short line, attempting to visualize how far in front of them weâ€™d be and wondering how much we'd be jet-blasting them when the inevitable takeoff clearance was given to us as the preceding aircraft. While paying close attention to Aircraft Y, I noticed their strobe lights were flashing, which, at least per our procedures, is a normal requirement when on an active runway. Due to our angle, in daylight conditions, and approaching at 90 degrees from their right, I wasnâ€™t able to detect whether or not the landing lights were on, which wouldâ€™ve been a more obvious clue they were issued a takeoff clearance. After visually confirming the approach path of runway XY was clear, my FO again queried tower to confirm our line up and wait instruction, to which tower replied "affirm." About the time the aircraft radome crossed the hold short line, my FO noticed the wheels of the 737 moving. He announced "Stop. Stop!" I looked over at him and simultaneously pressed the toe brakes and set the parking brake once the aircraft stopped. I said to him "I didnâ€™t hear line up and wait behind, I heard line up and wait." He acknowledged to me he heard the same thing from ATC. He again asked ZZZZ Tower to clarify the clearance and tower said it was a "line up and wait **behind**" instruction. My FO informed him that he issued us a "line up and wait" **only** clearance to which the controller responded, "ohh oops, my bad." We were then instructed to line up and wait from taxiway 2 and departed shortly afterwards without further incident.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air carrier pilot departing a foreign airport reported they were issued takeoff clearance from an intersection while another aircraft was beginning takeoff from the end of the runway.

1.Text: Flight xxxx ZZZ1-ZZZ2, level cruise at 340. ECAM message G HYD RSVR LO LVL with gauge indication of the green system fluid empty. Executed the ECAM procedure turning the PTU (Power Transfer Unit) off and the green engine pump off. Verified the inoperative systems and checked the FM for additional information. Attempted to contact dispatch via AIRINC but were unable due to frequency interference. Contacted dispatch via ACARS and advised them of the situation and intent to divert to ZZZ. Dispatch advised the would make all notifications. We then contacted ATC, requested priority handling and requested divert to ZZZ runway XXL. Flight attendants briefed accordingly and passengers were notified of the situation. No preparation for evacuation was made as I deemed it unnecessary. We then reviewed the landing gear gravity extension procedure, the overweigh landing procedure, obtained landing performance data and discussed the runway exit plans as the nose wheel steering was inop. The ILS for runway XXL was intercepted on a 17 mile final at 3000 MSL. The gravity gear extension was accomplished, the aircraft slowed and configured and an uneventful approach to the runway was accomplished. The aircraft was slowed to taxi speed and I determined I had sufficient control to exit onto the high speed taxi exit and parallel taxiway. The aircraft was stopped and communications established with Crash Rescue. Nothing was reported or observed. The company tug then made contact and aircraft was connected and tugged to the gate.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported during cruise flight receiving a ECAM message for G HYD RSVR LO LVL resulting in the flight crew diverting to the nearest airport where they landed safely.

1.Text: Not long after leveling off at cruise altitude from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 we experienced both a green hydraulic system low level and low pressure ECAM. I continued to fly the aircraft and took over comms while the Captain ran the ECAM. The ECAM directed us to turn off the PTU (Power Transfer Unit) and the hydraulic engine 1 pump. After completing the ECAM and consulting the flight manual and calculating landing distance, reviewing gravity gear extension procedures, and tow in procedures we coordinated with dispatch a diversion to ZZZ. We knew we would be landing overweight so we requested FL240 with ATC and requested priority handling after reviewing overweight landing procedures. We set up for a long final to runway XXL. The Captain took control of the aircraft after we turned direct to ZZZ. On about a 15 mile final I gravity extended the gear and the captain landed the aircraft. Emergency personnel were standing by as we vacated the runway using only rudder steering. Company X operations came out and towed us into gate XX after the assessment was made that we did not need any emergency services. We ended up landing around149,000lbs, roughly 8000lbs overweight.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 First Officer reported hydraulic system failure and diversion to nearby airport.

1.Text: Encountered an updraft causing the aircraft to accelerate and abruptly climb approximately 700-1000 feet, advised ATC of strong updraft and returned to assigned altitude, the flight continued with no further events Cause: N/A - ATC did their best to get us above the weather and deviate laterally around the weather

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 pilot reported an updraft while deviating around an area of weather, which resulted in an altitude deviation. The pilot regained control and returned to the assigned altitude and continued to the destination.

1.Text: Our HYD Y system totally depleted and cavitated on departure climb out of ZZZZ. All checklist were performed. Returned to ZZZZ for landing. After arrival and inspection by maintenance we were informed that a tightening screw separated causing the hydraulic system's depletion and cavitation.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 flight crew reported a hydraulic system failure during climb out and return to departure airport.

1.Text: The flight diverted to ZZZ1 due to increasing crosswind gusts at the destination and a developing fuel margin concern. During preflight planning, a threat-forward approach was used. The First Officer, dispatcher, and I evaluated the original flight plan, which had us landing near maximum gross weight with no alternate listed. Additionally, forecast gusts at the destination were near the aircraft's Flight Manual maximum crosswind limits. Given these conditions, we coordinated with dispatch to revise the plan to include a suitable alternate with improved margins. A thorough fuel and performance discussion was conducted during the approach briefing, including crosswind limits, landing performance with gust factors, and contingency planning should a go-around become necessary. The approach was conducted in high velocity, gusty crosswind conditions. The approach was primarily in IMC. Appropriate precautions were taken to balance gust additives with stopping distance considerations. The approach was turbulent, careful automation management was utilized to maximize pilot Situational Awareness. Below approximately 500 feet AGL, high crosswind gusts appeared to increase significantly and momentarily, requiring large control inputs, to maintain the desired flight path while remaining within stabilized approach criteria. During the flare, at approximately 20â€“10 feet AGL, with thrust just brought to idle, the aircraft encountered a strong sustained lateral gust that required substantial control inputs to maintain runway centerline. Simultaneously, the gust produced a noticeable performance increase, resulting in altitude gain of 20â€“30 feet. Based on recent performance training and anticipating the potential for an equally rapid loss of performance as the gust potentially subsided, along with the risk of airspeed decreasing below Lowest Selectable Speed, I immediately initiated a go-around. The gust began to subside and the aircraft did appear to momentarily descend. During the maneuver, careful attention was paid to pitch attitude to mitigate tail strike risk. Flap retraction and pitch changes were managed deliberately, ensuring a positive rate of climb prior to significant changes. Given that a possible go-around scenario had been thoroughly briefed in the context of our general fuel state, the wind conditions, and considering the largely IMC conditions associated with lower ceilings on the approach end of the field, the crew recognized that a second attempt (if unsuccessful) would introduce downstream fuel concerns. After coordinating and assessing the situation, we elected to divert to ZZZ1. The diversion was conducted in a smooth and controlled manner. The FOM diversion guide was utilized. Dispatch was notified. The crew was very efficient, having thoroughly discussed and prepared for this possibility during the threat forward departure and approach briefing. Threat forward briefings, and recent performance training were pillars in insuring a safe outcome. The diversion recovery guide was utilized upon landing. We departed ZZZ1 with additional fuel, and landed in ZZZ uneventfully.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported high velocity and gusty crosswind conditions during landing phase. Crew diverted to alternate and landed.

1.Text: During engine start, we received ENG1 GEN FAULT. We followed ECAM procedures and it came back online. I entered it in the ELB (Electronic Logbook), called Dispatch, and finished the procedure with Maintenance Control. We called for taxi, was cleared to Runway XX, taxied out, and departed. At approximately 1500â€™ both the FO (First Officer) and I noticed a sort of shimmy, as though the gear was still down, flaps were down, or maybe the speed brakes were out, but all was normal. It did not seem to me like an engine vibration and we didnâ€™t notice any parameters showing high vibes, so we continued. On climb out, beginning at ~3000â€™, received multiple transient ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE ECAMs. All engine parameters were normal on both engines and the thrust levers were perfectly aligned, so I felt that continuing was the best plan. On the 4th or 5th ECAM, it stayed up almost long enough to run the full procedure, but then it went away again. It came back again as we were passing ~23,000â€™. It was no longer transient and I decided we needed to start back to the field. I asked the FO to pass the info to Dispatch. They messaged back that they would get the ball rolling. ATC turned us back and began our descent. The ECAM cleared, but we had already started turning back so we continued. We requested priority handling in the turn back to ZZZ. To this point, both engines had been performing normally and it seemed like it may have been an indication issue. On level off, ENG 1 did not spool up, staying at flight idle. The plane commanded LEVER MCT (Maximum Continuous Thrust), and performance went into EO (Engine-Out). At this point, I asked the FO to request ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) support upon arrival. They said the trucks would be ready. We revisited procedures and both agreed that everything had been completed, to include a report to the (LFA) Lead Flight Attendant. We were vectored to the ILS XX, but the tailwind during the return pushed us too much and we were vectored around for further descent. Upon the next vectors, I thought ATC had requested a ten degree turn to the left, which I did and then our course was promptly blown too close to the localizer - apparently they had given me a RIGHT course correction. They vectored us out once again and gave us much more room to catch the localizer. We commenced the approach, and landed without any further issues. At some point, when were exiting the runway I smelled something odd, so I requested ARFF scan ENG 1 just in case there was something internal to the nacelle. ARFF completed the entire aircraft scan and reported no further issues with the FLIR. I requested to continue into the terminal, to which we were given clearance. At this point, a passenger got up and used the bathroom before the FAs could stop them. Once they sat back down, we continued to taxi to the gate, shut down normally, and deplaned the pax. Iâ€™m fairly certain, with everything going on and the previously transient ECAM, something was missed in the approach. We revisited the procedures, although we briefed the passengers later than I would have liked, making sure all the information was covered. I feel like everything was covered, maybe poorly and out of sequence, but so many things were happening that I was doing a lot just staying in front of the problem and making sure that I was prioritizing flying the aircraft. We were constantly checking in with each other to make sure each of us were up to speed and also SA.

2.Text: After ENG 1 started and stabilized, we received an ECAM: ENG 1 GEN FAULT. We completed the ECAM procedures, and the generator came back online. We contacted Dispatch, completed the ELB (Electronic Logbook) entry, and cross-verified the information with each other. We were cleared to taxi to Runway XX and subsequently departed. During climb, at approximately 1,000â€“1,500 feet AGL, we noticed a brief irregular vibration, similar to what it would feel like if a gear door were open or the speed brakes were partially extended. All system parameters appeared normal, and the vibration lasted less than 10 seconds. We elected to continue the climb. Beginning at approximately 3,000 feet, we received an ECAM: ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE. The message cleared few seconds later. We verified engine parameters, thrust lever positions, and associated indications; all were normal. We assessed it as a transient condition and continued the climb. The same ECAM message reappeared multiple times (approximately 4â€“5 times). Then the ECAM remained long enough to begin and finish the ECAM procedure, but it cleared again. At approximately FL230, the ECAM returned. We requested ATC to level off to properly accomplish the checklist and assess the situation. While leveling at approximately FL280, we decided to return to ZZZ. We immediately notified Dispatch via ACARS of the ECAM message and our decision to return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling with ATC and advised them of our intention to return, including souls on board and fuel remaining. ATC cleared us direct to ZZZ. Until and during descent, both engines initially displayed matched parameters within normal limits. However, while descending, ENG 1 remained at idle and did not respond as expected. The system prompted us to set the thrust lever to MCT (Maximum Continuous Thrust). Considering the ENG 1 condition and the overweight landing, we requested ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) support from ATC. We completed all required coordination with ATC, Dispatch, the flight attendants, and passengers. After setting up for the approach and completing the approach briefing, we requested vectors to allow time to accomplish the overweight landing checklist. Upon completion, we cross-verified all checklist items to ensure nothing was missed. We were vectored for the ILS Runway XX but were unable to intercept the localizer. Requested another vector, cleared for the approach. We landed on Runway XX and vacated the runway. We stopped on Taxiway 1 to allow fire trucks to inspect the aircraft. ARFF reported no abnormalities. We contacted Operations frequency to advise them of our situation and assigned gate. We then taxied to the gate, shut down the engines, and the passengers deplaned without further incident. Being only approximately 50â€“60 miles from the departure airport, the repeated ECAM messages and evolving situation created a high workload environment. It was not a comfortable experience operationally. In hindsight, I could have taken additional time to review the Manual more thoroughly and attempt to gain a deeper, more systematic understanding of the malfunction. We also could have delegated tasks more efficiently to better manage workload and reduce task saturation. This report serves as a reflection on the event and improvement. While we strive for precision and professionalism, we recognize that we are not immune to human limitations.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 crew reported numerous transient "ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE" ECAMS during climb-out. During descent for return to departure airport ENG 1 failed to accelerate when commanded, but the flight continued to a safe landing.

1.Text: Passing FL270 on climb out of ZZZ the right engine (#2) oil temp starting flashing amber and indicated 150-160 degrees C. The oil quantity dropped to 10qts and oil pressure to 170psi. For comparison #1 engine was 110c, 17qts and 280psi. After crew discussion decided to advise ATC and after looking at suitable airports decided to return to ZZZ. An uneventful arrival, approach and landing were made. We elected to land overweight vice delay landing due to engine issue.
